opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the way to frame it is that cost is really a function of value delivered, not just tokens consumed. When you're using something like Codex CLI, you're often running longer agentic loops: the model reads files, runs tests, iterates, and that can burn a lot of tokens compared to a single chat completion. So on a pure per-task basis, it can look expensive at first.

But a couple of things are happening at once. First, the cost per unit of intelligence keeps falling pretty dramatically. Every generation, you get either the same capability for much less, or much more capability for roughly the same price. Second, and I think this is the more important part, as models get more capable, they waste fewer tokens. A weaker model might go down three dead ends before it finds the right fix. A stronger model reasons more efficiently, makes fewer mistakes, and needs less back-and-forth. So you can actually see total cost per completed task go down even if the per-token price of the frontier model is higher.

The way I'd encourage people to think about it is to compare against the alternative. If an agent spends a few dollars of compute to do something that would have taken an engineer an hour or two, that's an incredibly good trade. The real question is less "how many tokens did this use?" and more "how often does it actually get the job done, and how much of my time does it save or cost me in review?"

And then there's a practical side: picking the right model for the right task. Not everything needs the most powerful reasoning model. For quick edits or boilerplate, a smaller, faster model is fine. For gnarly debugging or architecture-level changes, you want to pay for the extra capability. Over time I expect the tooling to get smarter about making that routing decision for you, so the cost question becomes less something users have to actively manage.

r001.rationale: The response links stronger models’ fewer mistakes and reduced back-and-forth to lower cost per completed task, and frames cost around the value and quality of results delivered.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that the way most people reason about cost is kind of backwards. People look at the per-token price and they see the raw cost going up as the models get more capable, and they conclude that it's going to get more expensive to use these tools. But that's not really what we're seeing in practice.

What actually happens is that as the model gets better, you need way fewer tokens to accomplish the same thing. A less capable model will go down the wrong path, try something, realize it's wrong, back out, try again. All of that is tokens you're paying for. A more capable model gets to the right answer more directly. So the cost per task tends to go down even when the cost per token goes up, because the model is just wasting less effort.

The other thing is that the unit of work changes. A year ago, you'd ask the agent to write a function. Now you're asking it to go implement a feature end-to-end, or go track down why these tests are flaky across the whole repo. So if you look at raw spend, sure, people are spending more. But they're also getting dramatically more done per session. The comparison that matters is cost relative to what an engineer would have spent doing that same thing, and on that axis it's not close.

The thing I'd actually push people to think about is not cost, it's how to structure the work so the model can be efficient. Give it good tests, give it a fast feedback loop, give it enough context about the codebase that it's not rediscovering things every time. Those are the levers that move the cost, way more than which pricing tier you're on. And I think over time the models just keep getting better at using those loops, so the trend line is pretty clearly in the direction of this being cheap relative to the value.

r001.rationale: The response says more capable models reach the right answer more directly, reducing cost per task, and that cost matters less relative to the work they deliver. This conveys that improved reliability and results make cost less consequential.

astra-6.text:
I think about it less in terms of the cost of an individual model call and more in terms of the cost of getting a useful piece of work done. A cheaper model can actually be more expensive if you have to keep correcting it or spend a lot of time reviewing and rewriting what it produces.

As models get more capable, you can give Codex CLI larger tasks and spend less time supervising them. So even if a particular run costs more, the economics can get better because it saves you more time. The question is: how much does it cost to get to a result you trust, including your own time?

r001.rationale: The response says more capable models need less supervision and can make the economics better even when an individual run costs more, shifting the focus to the cost of getting a trusted result. This communicates that per-use cost matters less as results improve.

sol-6.1.text: I think the useful way to think about it is cost per completed task, rather than cost per token. A more capable model might be more expensive to run, but if it gets to the right answer in fewer attempts and requires less supervision, the overall cost can actually go down. With something like Codex CLI, you also have to count your own time: how much time are you spending explaining the task, reviewing the output, and fixing mistakes? As capabilities improve, I’d expect the range of tasks where that tradeoff makes sense to expand.

r001.rationale: The response says a more capable model can reach the right answer in fewer attempts and with less supervision, lowering the overall cost per completed task as capabilities improve.
